Difference-in-Differences in Stata

Day 1 — from raw files to a credible 2×2

KDIS Summer Workshop 2026

Day 1 of 2

How today works

  • Everything on this screen is also running live in Stata — the slides carry the questions and the ideas; the console carries the proof.
  • You have the same files: follow along in programs/day1.do, section by section.
  • The full write-up, with every command and its complete output, is in the handout (day1.html). These slides are the skeleton; the handout is the record.

The question

A national government has been expanding subsidized public childcare.

Districts joined the program in different years.

Did the program raise maternal employment?

Today: one adoption cohort (2007) vs districts that never joined — one treatment date, one control group.

The classic setting.

Day 2: all districts at once — and everything we build today will break.

The same question, in any field

Program Outcome
public childcare maternal employment
forest conservation payments forest cover
anti-corruption reform bribery rates
minimum wage rise (Card & Krueger 1994) employment

One skeleton: a program switches on — at a date, for some units, not others.

Swap the nouns; the method is identical.

When is DiD even possible?

DiD needs variation on two dimensions. Miss either, and there is no design.

  • Treatment reaches some units but not others. If everyone is treated the same, there is no comparison group.
  • You observe them both before and after treatment. With no pre-period, there is no trend to difference out.

The two axes need not be place and calendar time. Duflo (2001): school-building intensity by region × birth cohort — not region × year.

Miss either dimension → no DiD.

By the end of today you can

  1. Turn three messy raw files into an estimation panel.
  2. Compute a DiD estimate from four sample means.
  3. Get the identical number from a regression — and know why they match.
  4. State precisely what parallel trends does and does not require.
  5. Decide what to cluster standard errors on.
  6. Read an event-study plot.
  7. Export a publication-quality table that rebuilds itself.

Part 1 — The design

Laptops closed

One picture — the DiD map — built in stages.

A question before each stage. Commit to an answer first.

(Invented round numbers, not today’s data.)

Question 1

What is the effect of the program?

The honest answer: we cannot say

“12” — or “the jump after adoption” — assumes the outcome would have stood still.

But it was already rising before anyone was treated.

How much of the 12 would have happened anyway?

Question 2

What information would let us answer it?

A control group

The missing object: the treated group’s path without the program.

The stand-in: districts that never adopted — lower down, but gaining at the same rate per period, pushed along by the same common forces.

Question 3

Now — where is the effect?

The arithmetic

Control gained +6 → counterfactual: 54 + 6 = 60 → effect: 66 − 60 = 6.

Identically: (66 − 54) − (48 − 42) = 12 − 6.

The difference of two differences.

And when is the 6 wrong?

What would have to be true for the 6 to be wrong?

A world where it is wrong

Something steepened the treated path — for them only, at exactly adoption time.

True counterfactual 63, true effect 3.

DiD still confidently reports 6.

Look at the pre-periods

Identical to the good world’s.

The two worlds differ only in the part we never observe.

No data can tell you which world you are in.

That is why what DiD rests on is called an assumption.

What is data, what is assumption

Piece of the map What it is Observed?
solid navy line treated outcome yes
solid gray line control outcome yes
12-point gap in levels permanent group difference yes — and harmless
dashed line treated path without program no — assumed
red bracket causal effect (ATT) only if the dashed line is right

The assumption, stated precisely

Parallel trends. Had the program not existed, the treated group’s outcome would have changed by the same amount as the control group’s outcome actually changed.

With \(y_{it}(0)\) = outcome in the world without the program:

\[ E\big[\,y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - y_{i,\text{pre}}(0)\;\big|\;\text{Treated}\,\big] = E\big[\,y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - y_{i,\text{pre}}(0)\;\big|\;\text{Control}\,\big] \]

Three things it does not say

  1. Not that the groups are similar. Level gaps are differenced out. Trends, not levels.
  2. Not that it is testable. It is a claim about a counterfactual post-period. Parallel pre-trends are supporting evidence — never proof.
  3. Not that nothing else changed. Common shocks are fine; the control group absorbs them. Fatal: something hitting one group only, at treatment time.

And when it holds, the estimate is the ATT — the effect on the treated, not the effect the program would have anywhere else.

The rest of today builds this map from real files

Map piece Today’s version
two solid lines raw trends plot
four observed points the four-means table
the arithmetic reg with an interaction
“how parallel, really?” the event study

When in doubt: which piece of the map am I looking at?

Part 2 — Building the panel

The big picture

Everything today is computed from one table: a panel, one row per district-year.

Ingredient Variable Feeds
outcome emp_rate the two solid lines
adoption year adopt_year treated vs control
district size pop_thousands weighting

Part 2 = three messy files → that one clean panel.

import → destring → reshape → merge → xtset

Three files, as the agency sends them

File Shape You must
childcare_employment_wide.csv one row per district, one column per year reshape, destring
childcare_rollout.csv one row per district merge m:1
district_population.csv one row per district-year merge 1:1

Step 1 — import everything as text

import delimited "${raw}/childcare_employment_wide.csv", varnames(1) ///
    stringcols(_all) clear
(encoding automatically selected: ISO-8859-1)
(18 vars, 180 obs)

Sounds perverse — but now Stata cannot silently mangle a column.

We decide what becomes numeric.

list district_id yr2004 yr2005 yr2006 yr2007 in 1/5, noobs abbrev(12)
  +-------------------------------------------------+
  | district_id   yr2004   yr2005   yr2006   yr2007 |
  |-------------------------------------------------|
  |       11001    42.54    46.08    45.22    43.93 |
  |       11002    50.99    52.26    52.33    51.97 |
  |       11003    53.66    50.49    53.15    55.48 |
  |       11004    48.99    47.30    50.01    50.01 |
  |       11005    53.33    52.71    53.02    53.41 |
  +-------------------------------------------------+

180 districts, 16 year-columns — all of it text, including the numbers.

Step 2 — destring refuses. Good.

destring yr2004, replace
yr2004: contains nonnumeric characters; no replace

The fix is always the same: look at the raw values.

The agency writes .. for missing. Blank it out, then convert:

qui ds yr*
foreach v in `r(varlist)' {
    qui replace `v' = "" if `v' == ".."
}
destring yr*, replace
destring district_id, replace    // else the merge breaks later
yr2004: all characters numeric; replaced as double
(5 missing values generated)
yr2005: all characters numeric; replaced as double
(2 missing values generated)
...
yr2019: all characters numeric; replaced as double
(3 missing values generated)

The “missing values generated” messages are not errors — they are the .. entries becoming proper missings.

Read them.

Step 3 — reshape to long

Every panel command wants one row per unit per period.

reshape long yr, i(district_id) j(year)
rename yr emp_rate
Number of observations              180   ->   2,880

180 × 16 = 2,880. The arithmetic should always check out.

If it doesn’t, stop and find out why.

Step 4 — merge, and let Stata check your beliefs

merge m:1 district_id using `roll'      // one row per district
merge 1:1 district_id year using `pop'  // one row per district-year
    Not matched                             0
    Matched                             2,880  (_merge==3)
  • m:1 vs 1:1 is a claim about the data. If it is false, Stata stops.
  • Never ignore _merge. Zero unmatched is the good case; anything else, find out which side and why before continuing.

Step 5 — declare the panel

xtset district_id year
Panel variable: district_id (strongly balanced)
 Time variable: year, 2004 to 2019
         Delta: 1 unit
tab adopt_year, missing
 adopt_year |      Freq.     Percent        Cum.
------------+-----------------------------------
       2007 |        720       25.00       25.00
       2010 |        720       25.00       50.00
       2013 |        720       25.00       75.00
       2016 |        480       16.67       91.67
          . |        240        8.33      100.00
------------+-----------------------------------
      Total |      2,880      100.00
  • Four cohorts — plus 15 never-treated districts (the . row, 15 × 16 = 240).
  • 53 missing outcome cells: balanced in structure, holes in the data.
  • Today: 2007 cohort vs never-treated only. The rest waits for Day 2.

Part 3 — Estimation

First: look at the data

This is the map, drawn by real data

  • The groups are miles apart in level (~56% vs ~42%). Harmless.
  • What matters: the slopes before 2007 — close to parallel.

“These groups look nothing alike” is not an objection. “These groups were on different trajectories” is.

Conventions worth copying:

  • collapse first, then plot
  • xline(2006.5) — the boundary, not the first treated year

The 2×2: four numbers

Years 2006 and 2012; joiners vs never-joiners.

table (treated) (post), stat(mean emp_rate) nformat(%7.3f)
        |            post
        |       0        1
--------+------------------
treated |
  0     |  41.737   44.165
  1     |  56.224   63.590
  Change for treated districts   :   7.366
  Change for control districts   :   2.428
  ---------------------------------------
  Difference-in-differences      :   4.938

From the equation to the command

\[ y_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Treated}_i + \beta_2\,\text{Post}_t + \beta_3\,(\text{Treated}_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it} \]

Term What it is Stata
\(\beta_0\) control, pre-period mean _cons
\(\beta_1\) permanent gap between groups i.treated
\(\beta_2\) common change over time i.post
\(\beta_3\) the DiD estimate i.treated#i.post
all three i.treated##i.post

## gives main effects and interaction.

# alone silently drops the main effects — almost always a mistake.

The regression is the same arithmetic

reg emp_rate i.treated##i.post
   1.treated |   14.48728    ...
      1.post |    2.42819    ...
treated#post |
        1 1  |   4.937845   1.442825    3.42   0.001
       _cons |   41.73714    ...
  • _cons = 41.737 — control pre-mean, exactly.
  • 1.post = 2.428 — the control group’s change.
  • treated#post = 4.938 — the hand-computed number, to three decimals.

The regression adds nothing to the arithmetic.

What it adds: a standard error — and covariates if we want them.

Standard errors: what to cluster on

reg emp_rate i.treated##i.post
reg emp_rate i.treated##i.post, robust
reg emp_rate i.treated##i.post, cluster(district_id)
  Default (homoskedastic) SE : 1.4428
  Robust SE                  : 1.2300
  Clustered by district SE   : 0.5959

Clustering shrank the SE here — it does not always inflate.

The rule: cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned. The program was assigned to districts → cluster on districts.

Using all sixteen years: fixed effects

\[ y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \beta\,D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} \]

Term Absorbs Stata
\(\alpha_i\) everything permanent about a district absorb(district_id)
\(\lambda_t\) everything common to a year i.year
\(\beta\) the effect coefficient on treat 
areg emp_rate treat i.year, absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
       treat |   5.591371   .2313964    24.16   0.000

Why bigger than 4.94? The 2×2 measured year five only.

This averages years 1–13 — and the effect grows.

The event study: the shape, not just the average

One dummy per year relative to adoption; omit \(k=-1\) as the reference.

areg emp_rate lead_3 lead_2 lag_*  i.year, ///
    absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
      lead_3 |    .190979   .5274014     0.36   0.719
      lead_2 |   .3015874   .4943579     0.61   0.544
       lag_0 |   .5309113   .4602404     1.15   0.253
       lag_5 |   5.288708   .5416055     9.76   0.000
      lag_12 |   9.562436   .4359017    21.94   0.000

The event study, plotted

Reading it — and drawing it

  • Left of the line: leads of 0.19 (p=0.72) and 0.30 (p=0.54) — the groups were not drifting apart before the program.
  • Right: not a step. Near zero in year 0, ~5.3 by year six, ~9.5 after a decade. Childcare centers take years to build.

Conventions readers will expect:

  • reference period plotted as an explicit zero;
  • vertical line at −0.5; horizontal line at 0;
  • confidence intervals always;
  • title = what it shows, not what you concluded;
  • export .png for slides, .pdf/.eps for journals.

Flat pre-trends are reassuring — not proof. On Day 2, this test will actively mislead us.

Part 4 — The publication table

Why you never type a number into Word

  • ~20 cells in the table × ~10 rebuilds before publication = 200 opportunities to mistype — and nobody proofreads a table twice.
  • Worse: when updating is tedious, you stop doing it, and the table drifts away from the text.

Every number in the paper must be traceable to a line of code. If you typed it, you cannot trust it.

Build: store as you estimate

eststo clear
eststo c1: qui reg  emp_rate i.treated##i.post, cluster(district_id)
estadd local yrs "2006, 2012"
estadd local dfe "No"

eststo c2: qui areg emp_rate tr i.year, ///
    absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)
estadd local yrs "2004-2019"
estadd local dfe "Yes"

eststo c3: qui areg emp_rate tr i.year [aw=pop_thousands], ///
    absorb(district_id) cluster(district_id)

estadd local writes the rows a DiD table is judged on:

  • which years, which fixed effects, which sample

  • they are not in the regression output; you add them.

One options macro — so versions cannot drift

local topts ///
    rename(1.treated#1.post DiD tr DiD) keep(DiD) ///
    b(%9.3f) se(%9.3f) star(* 0.10 ** 0.05 *** 0.01) ///
    coeflabels(DiD "Childcare program") varwidth(22) ///
    stats(yrs dfe yfe wgt N r2, ...)

esttab c1 c2 c3, `topts' mtitles("2x2" "All years" "Weighted")
esttab c1 c2 c3 using "${res}/table1_did.rtf", ///
    replace `topts' ...
esttab c1 c2 c3 using "${res}/table1_did.tex", ///
    replace booktabs `topts' ...

rename() maps 1.treated#1.post and tr onto one row.

Screen, Word, and LaTeX are literally the same options.

The result

                                (1)             (2)             (3)
                                2x2       All years        Weighted
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Childcare program             4.938***        5.591***        5.464***
                            (0.596)         (0.231)         (0.237)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Years used               2006, 2012       2004-2019       2004-2019
District FE                      No             Yes             Yes
Year FE                          No             Yes             Yes
Pop. weighted                    No              No             Yes
Observations                    116             939             939

4.9–5.6 points, stable across specifications. A genuine result.

On Day 2, every number in this table changes.

Rebuilding it will take one command — because the table is code.

If it lived in Word, all twenty cells would have to be found and retyped.

Take away

  1. Look at raw trends before you estimate anything.
  2. DiD is four sample means; the regression is bookkeeping for that arithmetic.
  3. Parallel trends is about slopes, not gaps — and it is an assumption, not a test result.
  4. Cluster where treatment was assigned.
  5. Event studies show the shape of an effect — and let others probe your assumption.
  6. Every number in the paper comes from code.

Next: the assignment — five exercises, also written out in the handout.

The assignment

The exercises

Work in groups. Each group finishes exercises 1, 2, 3, and 4 and submits before leaving; doing this on both days is what earns the workshop’s Open Badge. Exercise 5 is optional and not collected. Stuck is normal — ask now.

  1. Change the comparison window. Redo the 2×2 with pre-year 2005 and post-year 2019. Does the estimate go up or down? Explain why, using the event-study plot.
  2. A placebo test. Pretend the program started in 2005: drop all data from 2007 onward and estimate the DiD. What should you find — and do you?
  3. Weighting. Re-estimate the multi-period specification with [aweight = pop_thousands]. Does weighting by district size change the answer? Should it?
  4. Clustering, deliberately wrong. Run the multi-period regression clustering on year instead of district_id. How many clusters do you have, and why is that a problem?
  5. Add a column (optional — the long one, for your own time). Add a fourth column to Table 1 restricted to 2004–2015, with its own estadd local rows. Columns 1–3 stay untouched; the Word and LaTeX files should update on their own.

One do-file per group, top to bottom; answers as comments; submit the .do and the .log before leaving:

capture log close
log using "day1_hw_group3.log", replace text
display "Day 1 — Group 3 — Lastname, Lastname, Lastname"
* Exercise 1 — commands first, then your answer as a comment
log close
